title: Staggered fintech adoption on loan default rates

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Difference-in-Differences (with staggered adoption). Because every bank either never adopts or adopts the algorithmic‐scoring technology only once, the policy is irreversible and timing varies. A two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) DiD recovers the average treatment effect when treatment timing is homogeneous; but with staggered timing we also report the Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) estimator that is robust to treatment-cohort heterogeneity.

Key identifying assumptions  
• Parallel trends: in the absence of fintech adoption, treated and never-treated banks’ default rates would have evolved in parallel.  
• No anticipatory effects: outcomes are not affected before actual adoption.  
• Stable unit treatment value (no spill-overs across banks).  

## 2. R Code
```r
###############################################
#  Fintech adoption and loan default rates   ##
###############################################
# Packages
library(data.table)     # fast read / manipulation
library(fixest)         # TWFE DiD
library(did)            # Callaway-Sant’Anna
library(broom)          # tidy output

# 1. Read data --------------------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s08_data.csv"
df   <- fread(path)

# 2. Basic TWFE DiD  --------------------------------------------------------
# y = beta * Treat x Post  + unit FE + time FE
did_twfe <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period,
                  data = df, cluster = "unit_id")

twfe_res <- tidy(did_twfe, conf.int = TRUE)
cat("=== TWFE Difference-in-Differences ===\n")
print(twfe_res[, c("term","estimate","conf.low","conf.high","p.value")])

# 3. Staggered-timing robust ATT (Callaway-Sant’Anna) ----------------------
# define first-treatment cohort g (0 = never treated)
df[, g := ifelse(treated==1, 4, 0)]   # all adopters switch in q4 in this toy data
att_gt <- att_gt(yname  = "y",
                 tname  = "period",
                 idname = "unit_id",
                 gname  = "g",
                 data   = df)

# Aggregate ATT across post-treatment periods (“simple” = equal weights)
agg_simple <- aggte(att_gt, type = "simple")
cat("\n=== Callaway-Sant’Anna ATT (simple average) ===\n")
print(round(agg_simple$att, 4))

# 4. Event-study / dynamic effects (robustness) ----------------------------
# leads/lags relative to adoption
event_twfe <- feols(y ~ sunab(unit_id, period, ref = 3) | unit_id + period,
                    data = df, cluster = "unit_id")
cat("\n=== Event-study leads/lags (Sun & Abraham) ===\n")
print(coeftable(event_twfe)[1:6, ])   # show first few leads/lags

# 5. Placebo pre-trend test (periods 1-3 only) -----------------------------
pre_df <- df[period <= 3]
placebo <- feols(y ~ treated:factor(period) | unit_id + period,
                 data = pre_df, cluster = "unit_id")
cat("\n=== Placebo test (pre-adoption periods only) ===\n")
print(coeftable(placebo))
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: negative. Algorithmic credit scoring should improve screening, hence reduce default rates.

Magnitude: roughly −0.03 to −0.05 (i.e. 3–5 percentage-point reduction) on a mean default rate near 20–25 %. The TWFE coefficient and the Callaway-Sant’Anna average ATT are therefore expected around −0.04.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Staggered DID (Callaway-Sant'Anna or Sun-Abraham) — cohort-specific ATTs; treatment=fintech adoption
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Fintech-adopting banks reduce default rates relative to non-adopters
